title: Operational Amplifiers, Differential Shunt Amplification, Common-Mode Voltage & Kelvin Sensing

blocks.x: To control motor torque at $20\text{–}40\text{ kHz}$ in Tier 2 (`01-electronics.T2.02` and `03-sensors.T2.04`), your microcontroller must measure phase currents of $\pm 15\text{ A}$ across a tiny $R_{\text{shunt}} = 2\text{ m}\Omega$ resistor. That produces a signal of only $\pm 30\text{ mV}$ riding on top of a noisy power ground or switching phase node! Understanding how **operational amplifiers (op-amps)** and dedicated current-sense amplifiers (`INA240`) amplify microvolt differential drops around a $V_{\text{ref}} = 1.65\text{ V}$ mid-supply bias while rejecting common-mode bounce—and why **4-terminal Kelvin traces** are mandatory—prevents 50% current measurement errors on your first custom PCB. Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

blocks.caption: A shunt, an amplifier and an ADC: each stage narrows the range and adds its own noise to the same small reading.

blocks.x: Imagine trying to measure the height of a $3\text{ cm}$ ripple on the surface of the ocean while both you and the ripple are riding up and down on a $48\text{ m}$ tidal wave. The $48\text{ m}$ wave is the **common-mode voltage** $V_{\text{CM}}$ (shared equally by both ends of the shunt resistor), and the $3\text{ cm}$ ripple is the **differential shunt voltage** $V_{\text{diff}} = I \cdot R_{\text{shunt}}$. A **differential current-sense amplifier** (`INA240`) subtracts the two pins so the tidal wave cancels out (**Common-Mode Rejection Ratio, CMRR**), multiplies only the $3\text{ cm}$ ripple by gain $G = 20\text{ V/V}$, and centers the result at $V_{\text{ref}} = 1.65\text{ V}$ so the $0\text{–}3.3\text{ V}$ ADC can read both positive ($+15\text{ A}$) and negative ($-15\text{ A}$) currents. And why **4-terminal Kelvin connections**? Because if your sense traces tap into the heavy copper power pads where $15\text{ A}$ is flowing, even $1\text{ m}\Omega$ of solder/trace resistance adds a $50\%$ fake voltage error to a $2\text{ m}\Omega$ shunt!

items.x: **Ideal Op-Amp Under Negative Feedback:** With negative feedback active and output unsaturated, an ideal op-amp draws zero input bias current ($I_+ = I_- = 0$) and drives its differential input voltage to zero ($V_+ \approx V_-$, the **virtual short**).

**Bidirectional Differential Shunt Amplifier Transfer Function:** For phase current $I_{\text{phase}}$ ($\text{A}$) through shunt resistance $R_{\text{shunt}}$ ($\Omega$), amplifier gain $G$ ($\text{V/V}$), and mid-rail reference $V_{\text{ref}} = 1.65\text{ V}$, the ADC pin voltage is:

blocks.x: Substituting $V_{\text{ref}} = 1.65\text{ V}$, $G = 20.0\text{ V/V}$, $R_{\text{shunt}} = 0.003\ \Omega$ ($3\text{ m}\Omega$), and $I_{\text{phase}} = +15.0\text{ A}$ gives $V_{\text{ADC}} = 1.65 + 20(15.0)(0.003) = 2.55\text{ V}$ (and $0.75\text{ V}$ at $-15.0\text{ A}$). A common-mode jump $\Delta V_{\text{CM}}$ attenuated by $\text{CMRR}_{\text{dB}}$ adds input-referred error $\Delta V_{\text{err,in}} = \Delta V_{\text{CM}} \cdot 10^{-\text{CMRR}_{\text{dB}}/20}$.

items.x: **2-Terminal vs. 4-Terminal Kelvin Shunt Parasitic Error:** If two sense traces tap into the load current path with parasitic copper/solder resistance $R_{\text{trace}}$ ($\Omega$) on each pad, the apparent shunt resistance becomes $R_{\text{meas}} = R_{\text{shunt}} + 2 R_{\text{trace}}$, creating relative gain error:

blocks.x: Substituting $R_{\text{shunt}} = 2.0\text{ m}\Omega$ and $R_{\text{trace}} = 0.6\text{ m}\Omega$ gives $\varepsilon_{\text{gain}} = 1.2 / 2.0 = +60\%$ error! Tapping dedicated non-current-carrying inner Kelvin sense pads reduces $I_{\text{sense}} \approx 0$, eliminating the $2 R_{\text{trace}}$ drop.

**Predict first (before you run it):** Commit to three numbers and one ordering before you touch the code. (1) With $G = 20\text{ V/V}$, $R_{\text{shunt}} = 3\text{ m}\Omega$ and $V_{\text{ref}} = 1.65\text{ V}$, what are $V_{\text{ADC}}$ at $+25\text{ A}$ and at $-25\text{ A}$, and is the $\pm 25\text{ A}$ span inside the $3.30\text{ V}$ rail? (2) Which error is larger *measured in amperes of misread current* — the $40\%$ non-Kelvin gain error from $R_{\text{trace}} = 0.6\text{ m}\Omega$ per pad, or the $93\text{ dB}$ CMRR residue produced by a $48\text{ V}$ common-mode step amplified by $G = 20$? Write down both in $\text{A}$ before comparing. Two tells that your result is wrong rather than the module: the two endpoints must come out mirror images about $V_{\text{ref}}$, so an asymmetric pair means a signed current or a wrong reference; and a non-Kelvin error that lands *below* $40\%$ on a $3\text{ m}\Omega$ shunt means you charged $R_{\text{trace}}$ to one pad instead of both ($2 R_{\text{trace}}$).
Design a bidirectional current-sense stage using an `INA240A1` ($G = 20\text{ V/V}$, $\text{CMRR} = 93\text{ dB}$ AC) with $R_{\text{shunt}} = 0.003\ \Omega$ ($3\text{ m}\Omega$) and $V_{\text{ref}} = 1.65\text{ V}$ for $I \in [-25\text{ A}, +25\text{ A}]$, and compare the 2-terminal parasitic copper error ($R_{\text{trace}} = 0.6\text{ m}\Omega$ per pad) against a 4-terminal Kelvin layout.

import math

def shunt_adc_voltage(i_amp: float, r_shunt: float = 0.003, gain: float = 20.0, v_ref: float = 1.65) -> float:
    return v_ref + gain * i_amp * r_shunt

v_pos25 = shunt_adc_voltage(+25.0)
v_neg25 = shunt_adc_voltage(-25.0)
kelvin_err_pct = 100.0 * (2.0 * 0.0006) / 0.003
cm_err_mv = (48.0 * (10.0 ** (-93.0 / 20.0)) * 20.0) * 1000.0

assert math.isclose(v_pos25, 3.15, rel_tol=1e-9) and v_pos25 < 3.30
assert math.isclose(v_neg25, 0.15, rel_tol=1e-9) and v_neg25 > 0.00
assert math.isclose(kelvin_err_pct, 40.0, rel_tol=1e-9)
assert math.isclose(cm_err_mv, 21.5008, abs_tol=1e-2)
print(f"V_ADC(+25A)={v_pos25:.2f} V, V_ADC(-25A)={v_neg25:.2f} V, Non-Kelvin error={kelvin_err_pct:.1f}%")
V_ADC(+25A)=3.15 V, V_ADC(-25A)=0.15 V, Non-Kelvin error=40.0%

Verify $I_{\max} = \frac{1.65}{50.0 \times 0.001} = 33.0\text{ A}$ ($\pm 10^{-6}\text{ A}$).

[`exercises/01-electronics.T2.01a/`](../exercises/01-electronics.T2.01a/) turns this section into a test. `starter.py` holds seven holes: `shunt_adc_voltage` ($V_{\text{ref}} + GIR$), `shunt_current_from_adc` (its inverse, sign kept), `max_measurable_current` ($(V_{\text{rail}} - V_{\text{ref}})/(GR)$), `kelvin_gain_error_pct` ($100 \cdot 2 R_{\text{trace}}/R_{\text{shunt}}$), `cmrr_input_error_v` ($\Delta V_{\text{CM}} 10^{-\text{CMRR}/20}$), `cmrr_current_error_a` (the same residue over the shunt) and `adc_code` (a 12-bit, clamped unipolar code). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:

**34 tests.** The stage is checked at the worked example's $+3.15\text{ V}$ and $0.15\text{ V}$, at the mirror point about $1.65\text{ V}$, at $60\text{ mV/A}$, and at the exercise's $33.0\text{ A}$ with its $3.30\text{ V}$ boundary, so a dropped reference, a headroom measured from the rail, one-pad Kelvin copper, a voltage-ratio CMRR or a $4096$-count ADC each fail their own test. The transfer suite runs the stage on the workbench's own hardware: one count of the 12-bit ADC is $13.4\text{ mA}$ through a $3\text{ m}\Omega$ shunt and the plant only gets one decision per $1\text{ kHz}$ tick; the $50\text{ V/V}$ variant clips at $11\text{ A}$; the $40\%$ non-Kelvin error is worth $10\text{ A}$ at $25\text{ A}$ against the $93\text{ dB}$ residue's $0.36\text{ A}$ (and $1.33$ ADC counts); the module's $2\text{ m}\Omega$ shunt spends only $36\%$ of the $\pm 15\text{ A}$ range; and a REF tied to GND reports $0.00\text{ V}$ at zero current and clips every negative sample to code $0$. Five planted faults - `reference_dropped`, `kelvin_charges_one_pad`, `cmrr_amplifies`, `max_current_uses_rail_only`, `adc_code_uses_4096` - each fail the test named for them.

items.x: **Which quantity the exercise asks for.** The rail is symmetric about $V_{\text{ref}}$, so the positive swing left is $3.30 - 1.65 = 1.65\text{ V}$; dividing that by the stage's $\text{V/A}$ figure, $G R_{\text{shunt}} = 50.0 \times 0.001 = 0.050\text{ V/A}$, gives the current at the boundary.

**Why the answer is not $66\text{ A}$.** Measuring the swing from $\text{GND}$ instead of from $V_{\text{ref}}$ doubles the numerator; the amplifier's output can only rise $1.65\text{ V}$ above its zero-current point before it saturates at the $3.30\text{ V}$ rail.

**The check that catches both mistakes.** Feed $I_{\max}$ back through `shunt_adc_voltage`: it must land exactly on $3.30\text{ V}$, and $-I_{\max}$ must land exactly on $0.00\text{ V}$, because the two endpoints mirror about $1.65\text{ V}$.
**Keep the sign.** `shunt_current_from_adc` is the inverse of the stage, so the recovered current at $0.00\text{ V}$ is $-33.0\text{ A}$, not $+33.0\text{ A}$.

**What the suite refuses.** `shunt_adc_voltage` and `shunt_current_from_adc` raise on a non-positive shunt or gain, `kelvin_gain_error_pct` on a non-positive shunt or a negative trace and `cmrr_current_error_a` on a zero CMRR, `max_measurable_current` on a zero gain, zero shunt, non-positive rail or a reference outside it, and `adc_code` on a zero-bit or zero-rail converter - all `ValueError`.

blocks.x: Inject one realistic bring-up fault and diagnose it from the symptom alone, keeping $G = 20\text{ V/V}$ and $R_{\text{shunt}} = 3\text{ m}\Omega$:

items.x: **Inject:** leave the `INA240` reference pin tied to $\text{GND}$ instead of the $V_{\text{ref}} = 1.65\text{ V}$ mid-rail reference (the mistake in the `## 8. Common mistakes` table, made on purpose).

**Symptom:** the transfer function collapses to $V_{\text{ADC}} = G \cdot I \cdot R_{\text{shunt}}$, so $0\text{ A}$ now reads $0.00\text{ V}$ instead of $1.65\text{ V}$, $+25\text{ A}$ gives $+1.50\text{ V}$, and $-25\text{ A}$ wants $-1.50\text{ V}$, which the $0\text{–}3.30\text{ V}$ ADC clips to $0.00\text{ V}$ — the entire negative half of the bipolar range is gone.

**Diagnose:** the zero-current point localizes it. A gain, shunt, or Kelvin error still leaves $0\text{ A}$ sitting at the $1.65\text{ V}$ reference and only scales the swing, whereas a *shifted* zero that drops to $0.00\text{ V}$ and clips every negative sample can only come from the `REF` pin, so neither the shunt value nor the CMRR is suspect.

**Fix:** tie `REF1` and `REF2` together to a low-impedance $1.65\text{ V}$ source (a buffered `VREF/2` reference, not a high-value resistor divider that sags under the pin current), then prove it twice: short the amplifier inputs together ($0\text{ A}$) and the ADC must read $1.65\text{ V}$ to within $\pm 5\text{ mV}$, and drive $+25\text{ A}$ and confirm $3.15\text{ V}$, which is $0.15\text{ V}$ inside the $3.30\text{ V}$ rail.

`[Concept: opamp_negative_feedback_virtual_short]` Why is the virtual short an approximation rather than a law?

**A.** Because the op-amp's finite open-loop gain $A_{OL}$ leaves $V_+ - V_- = V_{\text{out}}/A_{OL}$; with $A_{OL} = 10^6$ and $V_{\text{out}} = 2\text{ V}$ the residual is about $2\ \mu\text{V}$, small only because the gain is enormous.
**B.** Because the inputs draw microamps through $10\text{ M}\Omega$ resistors.
**C.** Because negative feedback removes the input stage.
**D.** Because it only holds when $V_{\text{out}} = 0$.
`[Concept: differential_shunt_gain_and_cmrr]` A $12\text{ V}$ common-mode step shifts both inputs by the same $12\text{ V}$. What keeps it out of the measured current?
**A.** The shunt is grounded, so common mode cannot enter.

**B.** A differential amplifier rejects the common part in proportion to its CMRR - the matched input network and the amplifier's own rejection turn a $12\text{ V}$ shift into an output error of microvolts-to-millivolts, which is why resistor matching and an in-amp with specified CMRR both matter.
**C.** The ADC subtracts $12\text{ V}$ in software.
**D.** Common-mode voltage is a myth.
`[Concept: kelvin_four_terminal_sense_routing]` Why do the two Kelvin sense wires carry almost no current?
**A.** They are wound around a ferrite bead.
**B.** They terminate in the amplifier's high input impedance, so the $I R$ drop across their own copper and solder joints is negligible: only the shunt's own $I R$ appears across the sense pair.
**C.** They are made of superconducting wire.
**D.** The shunt is an open circuit to them.

`[Concept: parasitic_loop_inductance_voltage_overshoot]` Compute the overshoot $\Delta V = L_{\text{loop}}\,\Delta I/\Delta t$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) for $L_{\text{loop}} = 4.0\text{ nH}$, $\Delta I = 25.0\text{ A}$ and $\Delta t = 20.0\text{ ns}$.

`[Concept: bootstrap_high_side_gate_driver_and_deadtime]` The switching node sits at $V_{\text{SW}} = 36.0\text{ V}$ and the driver's bootstrap capacitor supplies $12.0\text{ V}$ above it. Compute the high-side gate voltage relative to $\text{GND}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).

`[Concept: precharge_resistor_inrush_and_tvs_clamp]` Compute the initial pre-charge current $V_{\text{bus}}/R_{\text{pre}}$ in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for a $60.0\text{ V}$ bus and $R_{\text{pre}} = 150\ \Omega$.

`[SAFETY] [Concept: precharge_resistor_inrush_and_tvs_clamp]` Compute the stored energy $E = \frac{1}{2} C_{\text{bus}} V_{\text{bus}}^2$ in joules ($\text{J}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $C_{\text{bus}} = 1000\ \mu\text{F}$ at $V_{\text{bus}} = 60.0\text{ V}$.
